## Brief

```markdown
# Brief: Can you run Things 3 on Windows, and what to use instead

Date: 2026-09-08

## Why this page

Audience and intent: Windows users, or Mac users adding a Windows machine, who currently use or are evaluating Things and need to know whether it runs on Windows and what their realistic options are. Intent is mixed solution-seeking and alternative evaluation, not brand purchase intent for our product.
Decision: Create, conditional on the existing-coverage check below. Demand evidence is one Australian month at 900; product fit is direct because our product runs on Windows and the searcher's blocker is platform availability. If an existing alternatives or comparison page already ranks for this intent, update that page instead of publishing a competing one.
Distinct value: An honest platform answer first, then a switcher-focused comparison written from actual use: what transfers from Things (projects, areas, today/upcoming planning, tags, repeating to-dos), what does not transfer cleanly, and what the migration path actually costs in time. Include a real, reproducible import walkthrough rather than a feature grid.
Existing coverage: No data. Inventory our alternatives, comparison and platform pages before writing, and name the page this one must not overlap with.
Desired outcome: Reader understands their options and starts a trial or download on Windows. Measurable outcome is Windows trial starts from this landing page.

## Search decisions

Primary query: things 3 for windows
Secondary terms and evaluator questions: is there a Things 3 Windows version, Things 3 Windows alternative, Things alternative for Windows, migrate from Things to Windows, Things 3 web version. Confirm each with a volume pull before committing; only the primary term has a supplied figure.
Title and H1 direction: Lead with the platform question and the practical answer. Non-brand and descriptive, for example "Things 3 on Windows: what is available and what to use instead". Do not lead with our brand name; the reader is not searching for us yet.
Description: State plainly that Things is not available on Windows, name the practical routes, and say what our product does and does not replicate. No overstated parity claims.
Canonical: Self-canonical on the single chosen URL. Do not spawn separate pages for "things 3 windows", "things 3 for pc", "things 3 windows download" and similar wordings; one page serves the intent.

Research evidence: see the metrics table above. Australian August 2026 volume 900 for the primary query. Global and US scope: No data. Exact prompt volume: No data (Exact unavailable); vendor Phrase 400 is context only. Property search data: No data.

## Editorial direction

North star: The reader should leave knowing there is no Windows build of Things, understanding the two or three genuine paths open to them, and able to judge whether our product fits their way of working.
Ideas to land:
- The direct answer to the platform question, in the first screen, with the current publisher position cited.
- Realistic workarounds and their costs, covering any web or remote-access route and why it may not suit daily use.
- What a Things user will recognise in our product and what they will have to give up or rebuild.
- What the migration actually involves, step by step, including any data that does not carry over.
Proof and limitations: Show the import with real screenshots or an actual exported file. State every feature we do not match, and say so before the reader finds out in a trial. If our cross-platform sync, quick entry or natural-language date handling differs from Things, describe the difference rather than the marketing summary.
Questions worth answering: Is there an official Windows version or a roadmap statement. Is there a web app. Can it run under emulation or remote desktop, and is that practical. What alternative is closest in feel. How do I move my existing projects and areas. Do I lose my repeating to-dos or tags. What does it cost. Mark any of these already answered elsewhere on the site and link rather than repeat.

## Sources and validation

Public sources: The publisher's official platform and system-requirements page, our own public product pages and documentation, and our public pricing page. No fetches were made for this brief, so the writer must open each source and record the access date.
Facts to verify before publishing:
- That Things is published for Apple platforms only, and that no Windows build or official web client exists as of the publication date. Confirm on the publisher's own site.
- The current state of any workaround the article mentions, tested by the writer.
- Every claim about our product's Windows support, sync behaviour, import formats and pricing, checked against the shipped product, not a roadmap or an internal feature list.
- That the import walkthrough works end to end on a current build.
Success measurement: Windows trial starts and activations from this landing page. Baseline: No data, page does not exist. Set the baseline after publication and review at 8 weeks against landing-page sessions and trial starts, filtered to this exact path.
```

## Recommended next evidence, in order

1. Existing-coverage check. Inventory current alternatives, comparison and platform pages and their query performance in Search Console for the property. This decides create versus update and is the cheapest blocker to clear.
2. A global and US volume pull for the primary and secondary terms. One Australian month at 900 is enough to justify investigating, not enough to size the opportunity. If Australia is the established market, say so explicitly and keep the scope label on every downstream report.
3. A results inspection for the primary query to confirm intent mix, which is currently inferred rather than observed. This determines whether the page leads with the platform answer or the comparison.
4. Volume for the secondary terms, which are currently unsourced.
5. Qualitative switcher evidence from support tickets, sales notes and community threads mentioning Things and Windows together. This is the evidence that makes the page distinctive and it does not depend on a vendor tool.
6. Prompt visibility. Exact prompt demand is unavailable from the current vendor, so do not report a prompt demand figure. If prompt visibility matters, run a documented, repeated prompt panel with engine, model, search mode, locale, date and repetitions recorded, and treat that as visibility evidence, not demand.

Confidence in the create recommendation: medium. The demand signal is single-market and single-month, and existing coverage is unverified. Product fit is the strong part of the case, since the searcher's blocker is exactly the constraint our product removes.
